Tillandsias / Slides

tillandsias · in one line

A small cloud region on your own computer.

Disposable workspaces. Durable work. Boundaries you can inspect.

Tools, services and AI assistants share one local region. Rebuild a workspace when needed; commit and push to keep your work.

The software is free. Your hardware, electricity and any paid AI service you choose still have costs.

tillandsias · the story

Three pillars: the workflow, its boundaries, and the host.

Containerized workflow

A forge holds the agent and its tools. Shared services provide the proxy, git mirror, secrets and local inference.

Linux security

Rootless containers and launch checks restrict the workspace. Egress, credential and supply-chain gaps remain.

Portable cloud region

macOS and Windows add a Linux virtual machine. Linux runs rootless containers on the host, sharing its kernel.

tillandsias · the shape

Containerization is not one layer.

Apps share a private network. On Mac and Windows, their containers run inside a Linux virtual machine; on Linux, they share the host kernel.

Each layer has its own job and lifecycle. Rebuild a workspace while keeping shared services and pushed work.

tillandsias · the boundary

One private network, and one guarded door.

The services an agent needs — the proxy, the git mirror, secrets, local inference — sit on a network with no route to the internet. Traffic that leaves goes through a single checked exit; everything else is refused rather than silently allowed.

This is the intended boundary. Egress and credential gaps remain; its protection depends on the checks actually enforcing it.

tillandsias · the decision

Push once. Keep a copy beyond your computer.

The mirror holds the upstream credential; your workspace never sees it. With an upstream configured, success means that upstream accepted the same refs.

No upstream? The push stays in the local mirror.

tillandsias · the whole workspace

One project. An orchestrated enclave.

tillandsias · from what it is to how it improves

Turn every change into a checked refinement.

The same loop works for code, specs, artifacts and documentation: state a constraint, make a small change, check it, and keep the evidence.

A prompt stops when it is close enough for this scope. More checked events increase refinement effort; they can reduce a non-zero skew in the remaining uncertainty, but this is an analogy to a weak law of large numbers, not a theorem about dependent prompts.

tillandsias · the how

Keep the target fixed while checking the next step.

At a fixed scope, checked evidence can advance along an ordered ladder. A release may change the target: compare scores only after accounting for that change.

A non-increasing residual bounded below has a limit. That alone does not show that the limit is zero, or that the implementation satisfies every real-world requirement.

tillandsias · the method

Short iterations, explicit evidence, room to be wrong.

Each run reads what earlier runs learned. Think of more events as a larger sample that may reduce a non-zero skew in the residual, while remembering that the prompts are dependent.

The weak-law picture is a useful intuition, not a convergence proof. The practical loop remains: make a small change, check it, seek a counterexample, and keep the correction in the record.

tillandsias · the working model

Small steps bring each part closer.

Accessibility, copy and dashboards each have a target. A small change, a check, then a recorded result: repeat that loop within each workstream.

Keep the checked gains and investigate setbacks. Each path can get closer at its own pace without being finished.

tillandsias · the working model

Progress in the parts adds up across the project.

With a fixed set of requirements and fixed weights, fewer gaps in each part means fewer gaps overall. Earlier gains remain while another workstream takes its next step.

If every local gap settles toward a limit, their fixed weighted total does too. That limit may still be above zero. Changed scope needs a new baseline; a better total never erases a local failure.

tillandsias · the how

Merge the same facts with the same rules.

Set union preserves distinct facts. A last-writer-wins register chooses one scalar value; it does not preserve every competing edit. The choice of merge rule matters.

Convergence needs the same delivered updates and a merge operation with the stated algebraic properties. It does not guarantee delivery, eliminate all git conflicts, or prove that a recorded claim is true.

tillandsias · keep what you learn

Many contributors. One accumulating evidence record.

Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) let contributors add distinct evidence events independently. Once everyone has the same events, merging them produces the same record, even after retries.

That supports the method: preserve what was learned, then check the next step. A failed check adds a correction or falsification; agreement on the record does not make its claims true.

tillandsias · collaborate and remember

Git carries the history. CRDT rules combine the record.

Commit distinct ledger fragments on each branch. Exchange and merge them through Git, then fold the delivered events into a shared view. Code and competing scalar edits still need their own merge rules and review.

Commits and tags let you revisit a recorded state. Mergeable version coordinates use a different rule: (2, 1) and (1, 3) join to (2, 3), taking each coordinate’s maximum. This illustrative join does not select a Git commit or prove release compatibility.

tillandsias · one project, many coordinates

Every artifact contributes a vector of evidence.

Files, specs, build artifacts and documentation evolve together. Here, a “vector” means their named requirements and evidence states.

Give evidence events stable IDs and merge them as a set. That record can follow CRDT rules across every artifact type. Git versions the files; ordinary file edits still need semantic review.

tillandsias · many histories, one bounded record

Many trees overlap toward a shared, bounded record.

Many branches of effort. One increasingly evidenced project.

Fix N requirements, each with seven evidence ranks. Inflationary steps keep or raise every rank; a monotone rule preserves their ordering. A fixed rule with both properties stabilizes within 6N strict increases — a bound on evidence states, not on commits, effort or elapsed time.

Each small Git history brings a different kind of evidence. Checked joins connect them into a shared refinement history within a fixed scope and finite evidence ranks; new scope or falsification opens an explicit new comparison. Tillandsias approximates this ideal through repeated effort: preserve checked gains, expose counterexamples, and reduce the remaining gaps. Monotonic convergence is conditional; its limit need not be perfection.
